newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Serb gets 20-year sentence for war crimes.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb gets 20-year sentence for war crimes.

text.p: The U.N. war crimes tribunal sentenced Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic to 20 years in prison on Monday for taking part in a vicious "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Moslem civilians.

Tadic, 41, a former police reservist nicknamed "Dusko", was given a total of 97 years on 11 counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the sentences will run concurrently with the longest single term.

He received the heaviest sentence, of 20 years, under an umbrella persecution charge covering beatings, torture and two brutal murders of Bosnian Moslems during the early stages of Bosnia's 1992-95 war.

"You committed these crimes with intention and with sadistic brutality using knives, iron bars, the butt of a pistol, sticks and...in one case tightening a noose around the victim's neck until he lost consciousness," presiding judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald of the United States said.
"To condone your actions is to give effect to a base view of morality and invite anarchy."
The trial chamber recommended the sentence should not be commuted or otherwise reduced to less than 10 years.

McDonald said Tadic showed a pattern of cruel and brutal conduct against his Moslem former friends and neighbours during a purge by Serb nationalist forces of Moslem and Croat inhabitants of the Prijedor area of northwestern Bosnia in 1992.

"You embraced the extreme principles of Serb nationalism," she said. "Those who sought territorial and political gains initiated a campaign to realise these goals by force of arms with limitless cruelty and viciousness."
"You responded to this campaign...and you must bear responsibility for your criminal conduct."
Tadic, dressed in a dark blue jacket and tie, looked pale and shaken as the sentence was read out. He waved briefly to supporters in the public gallery as he was led away.
He had faced a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, the term demanded by the tribunal's prosecutors. The court cannot impose a death penalty.
He has consistently denied all the charges. His lawyers have lodged an appeal against the verdict and intend to appeal against the sentence.
"We are disappointed, I think it is a very severe sentence," Tadic's lawyer Nikola Kostich said.
"What the court does is place Mr Tadic at the top of the ladder...The fact is that he was a very small player."
Monday's sentencing was the first after a full-length trial since the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) was established by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993.
The tribunal's prosecutors welcomed the sentence, saying it marked a significant step in the court's work.

"The victims who survived the crimes committed by Tadic will also no doubt welcome the tribunal's finding that he intentionally participated in the violent ethnic cleansing aimed at creating a greater Serbia and that he did so in a sadistic and brutal way," deputy prosecutor Graham Blewitt said.
"It should be remembered that the maximum sentence which can be imposed by the tribunal is life imprisonment. A sentence of 20 years imprisonment...is a substantial penalty."

The tribunal has issued indictments against 77 suspects -- most of them Serbs -- to date. But only 10 indictees, including Tadic, are in the tribunal's custody at its 24-cell detention unit in The Hague.

But NATO-led peacekeeping troops in Bosnia appear to have begun a more active pursuit of fugitive war-crimes indictees after years of criticism that they were doing little to support the tribunal's quest for justice.
Last week, crack British troops in Prijedor shot dead regional police chief Simo Drljaca after he resisted capture and arrested hospital director Milan Kovacevic.
Both were the subject of secret tribunal indictments in connection with the 1992 events in Prijedor. Kovacevic is now jailed in The Hague awaiting trial.

"The work of the tribunal is gaining momentum. The recent arrests of indicted accused has been a welcome development. The prosecutor will continue to take all available steps to bring other indicted accused persons to justice," Blewitt said.

The NATO swoop stirred speculation that the two most wanted war-crimes indictees -- former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and military chief General Ratko Mladic -- may also be snatched soon despite the fact that they have heavily armed guards around the clock.
Tadic, a former bar owner and father of two girls, has already spent three years in custody since his arrest in Germany where he was visiting relatives.

The Prijedor purge was one of the worst crimes against civilians in Bosnia's war. Non-Serbs, mostly Moslems but also Croats, were herded into three notorious prison camps -- Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje -- to be beaten, kept in inhumane conditions and, in some cases, executed.
The U.N. tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda mark the first attempt to try war criminals before a panel of judges since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.

Where Tadic will serve his sentence remains unresolved. Only two countries, Italy and Finland, have signed agreements offering to house convicted war criminals, but nine others have expressed willingness to do so.
